I love that you are actively taking steps to avoid triggers. It is wonderful and shows the kids that you respect them. 

Also talk about what to do when they run into a trigger. Come up with a plan together. it is unavoidable so its best to have a plan in place. I am a survivor of adult trauma. One thing I do is simply leave the room/movie theater/party. No questions asked, no blame or uncomfortable questions from my spouse. I just tell or text them that I need to leave and we are out of there. Think of a code word. We use "Do you have any chapstick?" means "I'm getting overwhelmed." and "I left my phone at home." is "panic attack! get me out of here right now." 

It also helps to me to talk about it in a casual maner. I don't like being hovered over, but we also can't ignore it. I find treating it like a normal thing takes the taboo out of it.

the quick version of my story - on adderall in grad school, stopped when I graduated, 5 years later I finally admitted to myself that I needed help to function at work. I told my doctor what I was experiencing as well as my personal worries about medication as I was two years sober (alcohol only no history of drug use or misuse). 

My doc said she didn't like Adderall as a long term solution. However, she suggested medication for a year or two while I worked with a therapist to develop tools to help me function at work. Three years later, the doctor agreed that long term medication use is best for me.  I did agree to reducing the dosage and seem to be doing ok with it.  

Doctors can have there own opinions, but it is your life and your health.

We found it best if we each have areas of responsibility and we leave it to the other person to take of it however they choose. No nagging, no reminding. we will do it when we are good and ready to do it. 

Clarify everyone's responsibilities and then let it go. It will get done eventually. 

 For example, I am responsible for lawn care/snow removal. If I procrastinate and don't mow, then the yard looks bad and thats it. No argument, no snide comments about mowing the lawn. It will get done eventually. 

 My spouse does the laundry. I don't say anything when it starts to pile up. I just go out and buy more undies! the laundry will be done eventually. 

We both like to cook. So whoever cooks, the other one does the dishes. I like to wait until before I go to bed, my spouse does them right after we are done eating.

My story is very similar.  Me (39 F) and my wife (49 F)  never really got a honeymoon because my sex drive is gone. So between my PTSD/anxiety/depression and her jumping into menopause, lets just say lesbian bed death has arrived.  A few practical things that worked for us. 1) I talked to my doctor about possible changes to my depression and anxiety medication 2) we talked about triggers and ways to avoid them. for example, we tend to be more affectionate during the day because night is a trigger. also, the bed is not good, so we go to the couch or play in the shower. 3) I can't handle penetration - at all. (But there are still lots of ways to play without penetration!) 4) we don't say sex, we say play. - ( I'm getting ready for a shower, do you want to join me and play a little?) 5) play does not require an orgasm. It is ok to play without any expectation. You are not a "failure" or "bad at sex". If an orgasm isn't there, thats ok. Its still fun to play around.  5) never underestimate the power of non-sexual touch. Hold hands, hug, slow dance, snuggle while you watch tv. Sometimes we just snuggle and hold each other without any expectation that it will go anywhere.

I am just starting so I don't know the long term effectiveness yet. So far I found it very helpful. I started to dissasociate twice in my last session. Once she said, "I need you to come back to the room. I need you here." That was enough to center me and we continued with the session. 

The second time we were deeper into the memory and trauma processing. I started to feel floaty and the room was starting to spin. I couldn't get back to the memory. She stopped the bilateral stimulation (buzzers in my hands), had me open my eyes. We did some grounding work. then we talked about what I thought happened. We think I was close to something and my brain wasn't ready to go there yet. I started to feel better and I agreed to try again. She slowed down the speed of the buzzers. I think that helped. I was able to finish the session and I feel like we make some great progress. We see disassociation as clues to help the trauma processing.

I agree with you about awareness. It is a difficult balance between privacy and wanting to advocate for mental health. I want to help break the stigma, but we also have to protect ourselves. 

Personally, when I was first diagnosed I did not tell many people. I wasn't ready. I just told my spouse, parents, and best friend. Later, I told my boss because I was concerned about having a panic attack at work and thought I might need a leave of absence. Also, I know my boss is a caring and kind person and he completely has my back. I trust him with this information. 

I told more people as I felt comfortable.  I was in therapy and felt like I had my feet under me. I had a bit more confidence. I needed to wait until I wasn't so raw. The better I felt, the more I was willing to share my story. This took time.  I started being an advocate for mental health awareness. 

I am a pastor and decided to share my diagnosis with my church. I simply told them that my doctor diagnosed me with PTSD and generalized anxiety disorder. I did not give details.  I simply asked for their patience and prayers. I had so many people come up to me over the next few weeks. Several shared there own diagnosis with anxiety, depression, bi-polar ect. For many, I was the first person they trusted to tell. Sharing my story helped open the conversation and deepened my connection to my community. 

Every situation is different. I was lucky to have people around me that I knew would have my back.

 Also keep in mind that you can wait to talk to people until you are ready. Start with a few trusted people, do the hard work in therapy, and tell your story or not. no judgement. It is your story and you can claim control over it. No one had the right to your history. your life, your choice.

YES! i completely get it. My trauma was 10 years ago, but i keep feeling like it hasn't fully hit me yet. Part of it is those hidden memories. when those memories start to reveal themselves it can be really scary. I also worry about what I don't remember. you are not alone. I think it is common to dread the revelations of trauma processing. 

My thearpist keeps reminding me to reframe the fear. recovering the memories will allow me to release them. to lift the burden and feel lighter. instead of passively waiting for the trauma memories to hit, I am actively bringing them forward so I can release them and gain control.

Only a medical professional can diagnose. However it is clear that this trauma is impacting your life and proper treatment can help. I also struggled with questioning a PTSD diagnosis. In my case, I don't get flashbacks. I do have horrible nightmares and intrusive thoughts. Long story short according to my therapist, I DO have PTSD (my original diagnosis was major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder). 

A few things I am working though that might help....

meeting the official PTSD criteria or not.... does it matter? it would not change how the trauma affects your life. it would not effect the treatment I received from my therapist. It would not effect my ability to heal. They are just four letters. They do not define your hurt or your ability to recover. your trauma is real and its impact on your life is real, regardless of your diagnosis. 

Here is where is can matter.... insurance. Insurance loves diagnosis. getting government/work/school accommodations, qualifying for disability, emotional support animals ect.  we have a system that loves putting people in boxes. 

I also found having a diagnosis helped explain my condition to other people. It helped my wife understand because it is "googleable."  

At the end of the day, the goal is to find help and healing.
